Lab 9

Gravity and movement

Build a field of blocks, give them mass and friction, and drive a bar through them with two keyframes; then roll a ball down a ramp into a row of dominoes. Twenty-seven small steps, every one animated.

Start the lab

Rendered in Blender by following the steps in this lab.

Today

We are learning

how Blender’s Rigid Body physics makes things fall, collide and push: the three kinds of rigid body (Active, Passive, Passive + Animated), the collision shapes, what mass and friction do, how two keyframes drive a sweeper through a field of blocks, and how a ball on a ramp starts a chain reaction.

You need Blender 4.2 or newer (this lab was built in 5.2), a mouse with a scroll wheel and a middle button (laptop trackpad? see this fix), and about two lessons. Save your files as Lab9A_Sweeper_YourName.blend and Lab9B_Dominoes_YourName.blend.

You’ve got it when you can

  • build a scene by typing numbers, and put a cube’s bottom exactly on the floor
  • say which rigid body type an object needs, and which collision shape, and why
  • keyframe a sweeper at two frames, play the simulation from frame 1, and bake it
  • light a scene with a sun and a sky, place a camera by number, render a still and an .mp4
  • build a domino run and explain what the gap, the friction and the ball’s mass each do

The plan

Five parts, 27 small steps. Each part ends with a picture of what yours should look like.

  1. Part 1Sweeper, floor, one blockSteps 1–5
  2. Part 2Physics on all threeSteps 6–9
  3. Part 3The sweepSteps 10–13
  4. Part 4Light, camera, renderSteps 14–17
  5. Part 5Part B: the domino runSteps 18–27

Three kinds of rigid body

Everything that moves in this lab is moved by the physics engine, and the physics engine only knows three kinds of thing. Active bodies have mass: gravity pulls them, collisions push them, and the engine decides where they are on every frame. Passive bodies are the walls and floors of the world: they stop things and never move. Passive + Animated bodies are the trick: they move where you keyed them, and the engine shoves everything Active out of their way. A sweeper, a piston, a hand, a car: anything that must move on cue and push things is Animated.

Then two numbers do most of the rest: mass (how hard something hits) and friction (how well it grips). And one choice that students get wrong most: the collision shape, which is the simple solid the engine uses instead of your mesh.

Word bank — open this if a word in the steps is new
Rigid Body
Physics for solid objects that do not bend. Added in the Physics tab.
Active
A rigid body with mass. Gravity and collisions move it.
Passive
A rigid body that never moves. Floors, walls, ramps.
Animated
A tick on a Passive body: it follows its keyframes and pushes Active bodies.
Collision shape
The simple solid the physics uses instead of the real mesh: Box, Sphere, Convex Hull, Mesh.
Mass
How much stuff is in it, in kilograms. Changes how hard it hits, not how fast it falls.
Friction
Grip between two surfaces, 0 (ice) to 1 (rubber). Both objects’ numbers count.
Bounciness
How much of the speed comes back after a hit: 0 a lump of clay, 1 a superball.
Keyframe
A saved value at one frame, shown as a yellow box or diamond. Blender fills in the frames between.
Cache / Bake
The stored result of the simulation. Bake works out every frame once and locks them.
Sun
A light that is a direction, not a place: the same everywhere in the scene.
World
The sky: a colour that lights everything a little and shows behind the scene.
Rename (F2)
A small box for typing the selected object’s name. Not F3, which is Search.
Cycles / EEVEE
Blender’s two renderers: Cycles traces light slowly and accurately, EEVEE draws fast like a game.
Chain reaction
One small push releases energy stored in the next thing, which pushes the next. Dominoes.

Part 1

The sweeper, the floor and one block

Tools: File › New, the N sidebar, Add › Mesh › Plane and Cube, F2, three materials.

Nothing in this lab is dragged into place. The Word version of Lab 9A said “press S then X” and “press G to position it accordingly”; here every object has numbers, so everyone’s sweep comes out the same and the physics can be reasoned about. Five steps build three objects; the fifteen blocks are copies of one.

How the steps work

Each step has a Where line (which part of the Blender window to look at), a Watch animation of the mouse doing the step (pause it, drag the slider, or use the arrow buttons to go one move at a time), and a Do this list of the same moves as a, b, c. The drawings are simplified, not screenshots: the words, numbers and positions match Blender; colours and spacing may not. A gold outline marks a box you type into; Blender itself keeps it grey. Orange, yellow and green boxes mean something real in Blender (changed, keyed here, keyed elsewhere): you meet them in Steps 10 and 11.

Two keys that look alike. F2 renames the selected object: a small box opens, you type the name, Enter. F3 is Search, for finding tools. Every name in this lab (Sweeper, Floor, Block, Domino, Ramp, Ball) is typed into the F2 box; none of them is a tool.

  1. Start fresh and save

    Layout workspace › the File menu at the very top-left.

    Do this:

    1. a
      File › New › General. Keep the cube: it becomes the sweeper. Keep the camera and the light too.
    2. b
      File › Save As. Find your Lab 9 folder, type Lab9A_Sweeper_YourName and click Save Blender File.
    3. c
      From now on press Ctrl+S every few steps, and always before you press Play.

    You should now see: the default cube on the grid, and your file name in the window title.

  2. The cube becomes the sweeper

    The viewport, then the N sidebar › Item tab.

    Predict first: A cube is 2 m across and its origin is in its middle. With Scale Z 0.3 it is 0.6 m tall: what Location Z puts its bottom exactly on the grid?

    Do this:

    1. a
      Click the cube (orange outline). N for the sidebar. Scale X 5, Y 0.3, Z 0.3, Enter after each: a bar 10 m long and 60 cm square.
    2. b
      Location Y -9: the bar moves to the near edge of the grid. Location Z 0.3: it rests on the grid instead of sinking half through it.
    3. c
      F2: the Rename box. Type Sweeper, Enter.

    You should now see: a long bar lying along X at the near edge of the grid, named Sweeper in the Outliner.

    Why numbers instead of S then X?

    The Word lab said “press S, then X” and drag until it looked right, so every student got a different bar and a different sweep. Scale X 5 on a 2 m cube is exactly 10 m; everyone’s sweeper is the same, and the numbers in the rest of the lab (where the blocks go, how far the bar travels) come out right.

  3. The floor

    Add › Mesh › Plane, then the N sidebar › Item tab.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Add › Mesh › Plane. A 2 m square appears at the cursor.
    2. b
      Sidebar: Scale X 12, Y 12, Z 12. A 24 m floor. The sweeper lies 3 m in from its near edge.
    3. c
      F2: Floor, Enter.

    You should now see: a big pale square with the bar lying across its near end.

    Why so big?

    The sweeper travels 18 m (from Y -9 to Y 9) and the pushed blocks end up a little past it. A 24 m floor leaves 3 m spare at each end, so nothing falls off the edge during the sweep.

  4. One block

    Add › Mesh › Cube, then the N sidebar › Item tab.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Add › Mesh › Cube. Sidebar: Scale X 0.25, Y 0.25, Z 0.25. A 50 cm block.
    2. b
      Location X -3, Y -3, Z 0.25. Six metres in front of the sweeper, at the left end of what will be a field of blocks; its bottom exactly on the floor.
    3. c
      F2: Block, Enter.

    You should now see: a small block on the floor, 6 m ahead of the sweeper and 3 m left of centre.

    Why Z 0.25?

    Same rule as the sweeper: Location Z = Scale Z puts the bottom of a cube on the floor. The Word lab’s cube was dragged into place and ended up half under the plane, then moved by eye. A block that starts inside the floor gets kicked out by the physics on frame 1 and the whole sweep goes wrong.

  5. Three materials, before any copying

    Properties editor › the red sphere Material tab

    Do this:

    1. a
      Block selected. Material tab › New. Name Red. Base Color › click the swatch › Hex › D93025. Roughness 0.4.
    2. b
      Click the Sweeper. New › name Blue › Hex 2B6CB0. Roughness 0.35.
    3. c
      Click the Floor. New › name Floor › Hex F0EDE6. Roughness 0.8. Pale, so shadows show on it.

    You should now see: faint colours in Solid view (press Z › Material Preview to see them properly): a red block, a blue bar, a pale floor.

    Why now?

    Step 9 makes fourteen copies of the block, and Shift+D copies the material along with everything else. Colour the one block now and the field colours itself. The Word lab coloured the block after copying, so every copy had to be done again.

End of Part 1. Save. Say which of the three objects will move on its own, which will be pushed, and which will never move.

Part 2

Physics on all three

Tools: Rigid Body: Active, Passive, and Passive + Animated; Box and Mesh collision shapes; Friction; Shift+D.

Three rigid bodies, three kinds. The block is Active: gravity and collisions move it. The floor is Passive: it catches. The sweeper is Passive and Animated: it goes where its keyframes say and shoves everything Active out of its way. The collision shape is a separate choice, and the Word lab got it wrong twice.

  1. The block: Active

    Properties editor (bottom right) › the blue orbit Physics tab (near the bottom of the tab column)

    Do this:

    1. a
      Click the Block. Physics tab › Rigid Body. Type Active: gravity pulls it, things push it.
    2. b
      Mass 20. Collisions › Shape Box.
    3. c
      Open Surface Response: Friction 1.

    You should now see: a Rigid Body panel on the Block reading Active, 20 kg, Box, Friction 1.

    Box, not Mesh. And why friction 1?

    The collision shape is the simple solid the physics engine uses instead of your mesh. For a cube, Box is exact and the fastest thing there is; Mesh (the Word lab’s choice) is slow and only needed for shapes with holes. Friction is grip: at the default 0.5 a pushed block skates on after the bar stops; at 1 it stays where it is left. Try the slider below.

    Friction

    A bar pushes a block at the sweeper’s speed and stops. Drag the friction and press Push.

  2. The floor: Passive

    Properties editor (bottom right) › the blue orbit Physics tab (near the bottom of the tab column)

    Do this:

    1. a
      Click the Floor. Physics tab › Rigid Body. Type Passive: it stops things and nothing moves it.
    2. b
      Collisions › Shape Mesh. A plane has no thickness for a Box to fit, so the plane itself is the shape.
    3. c
      Surface Response › Friction 1, to match the blocks.

    You should now see: a Rigid Body panel on the Floor reading Passive, Mesh, Friction 1. (Passive bodies have no Mass row.)

    What if the floor had no rigid body?

    The physics engine only knows about rigid bodies. A plane without one is scenery: the blocks fall straight through it on frame 2 and keep falling for ever. The first thing to check when something drops through something: does the thing it dropped through have a Rigid Body?

  3. The sweeper: Passive and Animated

    Properties editor (bottom right) › the blue orbit Physics tab (near the bottom of the tab column)

    Predict first: If the sweeper were Active instead, with a mass of 1 kg, what would happen when it met twenty kilograms of block?

    Do this:

    1. a
      Click the Sweeper. Physics tab › Rigid Body. Type Passive.
    2. b
      Tick Animated. This is the whole trick of the lab.
    3. c
      Collisions › Shape Box.

    You should now see: a Rigid Body panel on the Sweeper reading Passive, Animated ticked, Box.

    What does Animated do?

    A Passive body normally stands still. Animated means: this body goes exactly where its keyframes say, and the physics reads its position every frame and pushes any Active body out of its way. The sweeper cannot be slowed by the blocks, however many pile up: the keyframes win. The card at the top of the page has all three kinds side by side.

  4. A field of fifteen

    The viewport.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Block selected. Shift+D, then X, type 1.5, Enter: a copy 1.5 m along X. Do it four times: a row of five, X -3 to 3.
    2. b
      Select the whole row: click one block, Shift-click the other four (all five orange).
    3. c
      Shift+D, Y, 2.5, Enter: a second row 2.5 m further from the sweeper. Once more: three rows. Fifteen blocks, Block to Block.014 in the Outliner.

    You should now see: a 5 × 3 field of red blocks between Y -3 and Y 2, all with the Rigid Body and the material of the first. Checkpoint A below.

    Why copies and not fifteen new cubes?

    Shift+D copies everything about the object: size, material, rigid body settings. Fifteen fresh cubes would each need Steps 4, 5 and 6 again. The Word lab said “press Shift+D to duplicate it” once; where the copies go was left to the student.

Every rigid body in the lab on one table. Come back here whenever a step says “the same recipe”.

Part 3

The sweep

Tools: the Timeline, I to insert keyframes, Space, and Bake.

Two keyframes, 129 frames apart. Blender slides the sweeper between them; the physics does everything else. The first play is the simulation; the bake locks it in so the render can trust it.

  1. Key where the sweeper starts

    the Timeline along the bottom of the window and the viewport.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Timeline: the frame box reads 1 (Shift+← if not). Click the Sweeper.
    2. b
      Mouse over the viewport, press I. The sidebar Location boxes turn yellow and a diamond appears on frame 1. (Older Blender shows a menu: choose Location.)

    You should now see: the sidebar Location row yellow, a diamond at frame 1 in the timeline.

    What is a keyframe?

    A saved value at one frame: “on frame 1 the sweeper is at Y -9”. Yellow means keyed on this frame; green means keyed on another frame; orange means changed since the last key and about to be lost. Two keys and Blender draws every frame between them.

  2. Key where it ends

    the Timeline along the bottom of the window, then the N sidebar › Item tab.

    Predict first: 18 m in 129 frames: how fast is the sweeper in metres per second? Could you walk that fast?

    Do this:

    1. a
      Timeline: End 160. Frame box: 130, Enter. The blue marker jumps.
    2. b
      Sidebar: Location Y 9, Enter. The sweeper jumps to the far edge; the box turns orange.
    3. c
      Mouse over the viewport, I. Yellow, and a second diamond at 130. Drag the marker back and forth: the bar slides 18 m across the floor, straight through the blocks.

    You should now see: two diamonds in the timeline, and a sweeper that scrubs from one end of the floor to the other.

    Why 130, and why does it go through the blocks?

    The Word lab used frame 130 too: 129 frames at 24 a second is 5.4 s, so the bar moves at 3.4 m/s, a brisk walk. End 160 leaves 30 frames to watch the pile settle. Scrubbing passes through the blocks because the physics has not been run yet: it only computes when the film plays forward from frame 1.

  3. Play the sweep

    The viewport and the Timeline along the bottom of the window.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Shift+←: frame 1. Mouse over the viewport, Space.
    2. b
      Watch: the bar reaches the first row around frame 48. Blocks tip, tumble and bunch up against it; the second row joins at 70, the third at 84.
    3. c
      Frame 130: the bar stops at the far edge with all fifteen heaped in front of it. Space to pause, Shift+← to rewind.

    You should now see: a pile of red blocks shoved across the floor by a blue bar. Not matching? See the blocks fall through the floor, the bar passes through the blocks or the blocks fly everywhere. Checkpoint B below.

    Is the first play the simulation?

    Yes. The first time the film plays forward, Blender works the physics out frame by frame and keeps the answer in a cache. After that it just replays. Change a mass, a key or a shape and the cache is thrown away; play from frame 1 again.

  4. Bake it

    Properties editor › the cone-and-ball Scene tab.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Scene tab › Rigid Body World › Cache: End 160.
    2. b
      Click Bake. A progress bar runs; the button becomes Delete Bake.
    3. c
      Scrub anywhere: the pile is always right.

    You should now see: the Cache panel showing Delete Bake.

    Why bake?

    Rendering jumps straight to each frame, and an unbaked rigid body can only be computed in order from frame 1. Baked, every frame is stored and the render is trustworthy. Changed something afterwards? Delete Bake, play once, Bake again.

End of Part 3. Save. Watch the sweep once more and count on which frame the last row is hit.

Part 4

Light, camera, render

Tools: the Light and World tabs, the camera by number, Cycles for a still, EEVEE for the movie.

A sun, a sky and a camera that sees the whole run; then one Cycles still of the pile and a 160-frame EEVEE movie. The Word lab said “change the colour and lighting as necessary” and “render your file”; here it is four steps with numbers.

  1. A sun and a sky

    The Outliner, the green bulb Data tab, the N sidebar › Item tab and the red globe World tab.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Outliner › click Light. Data tab: click Sun. Strength 3.
    2. b
      Sidebar: Rotation X 50, Y 10, Z -60. Sunlight from the front-left.
    3. c
      World tab › Color › Hex B8C6D4: a pale sky, so the shadows are soft blue instead of black.

    You should now see: in Rendered view (Step 16) a pale sky and long soft shadows behind the blocks.

    Why a sun?

    The default point light is a bare bulb a few metres up: bright in the middle, dark at the edges of a 24 m floor. A sun is a direction, not a place: every block gets the same light and the same shadow, which is what an outdoor scene needs.

  2. The camera

    The Outliner, the N sidebar › Item tab, and the green camera Data tab.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Outliner › Camera. Sidebar: Location X -17, Y -14, Z 9.
    2. b
      Rotation X 69, Y 0, Z -49. Data tab: Focal Length 32.
    3. c
      Numpad 0: through the camera. The sweeper at the lower right, the field in the middle, the far edge of the floor at the top.

    You should now see: the camera view with the whole sweep in frame, start to finish. Not matching? See Numpad 0 shows nothing useful.

    Why there?

    Front-left and high, so the bar is seen moving away from the camera and the pile grows in front of it. 32 mm is a wide lens: the whole 18 m run fits. The numbers were found by trying; yours can differ once the sweep is in frame.

  3. A still of the pile (Cycles)

    The viewport, the Render tab, then the render window and its Image menu.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Mouse over the viewport, Z › Rendered. Frame box: 84, mid-sweep.
    2. b
      Render tab › Render Engine Cycles. Sampling › Render › Max Samples 64, Denoise ticked. F12: a minute or so.
    3. c
      In the render window: Image › Save As › PNG. Name it Lab9A_Sweeper_YourName_render, next to your .blend.

    You should now see: a photo of the pile halfway across the floor, with the sun’s shadows. Checkpoint C below.

    Cycles or EEVEE? GPU or CPU?

    The Word lab muddled two choices. Cycles and EEVEE are the two renderers: Cycles traces real light, slowly; EEVEE draws fast, like a game. GPU or CPU is which chip Cycles uses, under Render tab › Device; it only changes speed, not the picture. Use Cycles for the still because it is one frame; use EEVEE for the movie because it is 160.

  4. The movie (EEVEE)

    The Render tab, the Output tab, then the Render menu in the top bar.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Render tab › Render Engine back to EEVEE. Output tab › Resolution 50%.
    2. b
      Output panel: Media Type Video. Encoding › Container MPEG-4. The folder box: your Lab 9 folder.
    3. c
      Render › Render Animation (or Ctrl+F12). 160 frames: a few minutes. Then Ctrl+S. Part A is done.

    You should now see: a file called 0001-0160.mp4 in your folder: the sweep, start to finish.

    Why 50%?

    A quarter of the pixels, a quarter of the time, and it looks fine on a screen. Media Type Video is the setting the Word lab left out: on Image, Render Animation makes 160 separate pictures and no movie.

Part 5

Part B: the domino run

Tools: everything above, plus a ramp (a rotated plane), a Sphere collision shape and Bounciness.

The Word lab’s Section B was a link to a video. This Part B is a second scene made with the same tools: twelve Active tiles in a row, a Passive ramp, and a heavy Active ball that rolls down it and starts a chain reaction. Ten steps, most of them things you have already done once.

  1. A second file and a floor

    The File menu, then Add › Mesh › Plane, the N sidebar › Item tab and Properties editor (bottom right) › the blue orbit Physics tab (near the bottom of the tab column).

    Do this:

    1. a
      File › New › General. Click the cube, X › Delete. File › Save As: Lab9B_Dominoes_YourName.
    2. b
      Add › Mesh › Plane. Sidebar Scale 10, 10, 10. F2: Floor.
    3. c
      Physics › Rigid Body: Passive, Shape Mesh, Surface Response › Friction 1. The same floor recipe as Step 7.

    You should now see: a 20 m floor with a Passive rigid body, in a file named for Part B.

    Why a new file?

    Two scenes, two files: the sweeper is finished and handed in as it is. Part B uses the same three ideas (Active, Passive, a collision shape) on a chain reaction, which is what the Word lab’s “Section B” video was about.

  2. The first domino

    Add › Mesh › Cube, then the N sidebar › Item tab, Properties editor (bottom right) › the blue orbit Physics tab (near the bottom of the tab column) and Properties editor › the red sphere Material tab.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Add › Mesh › Cube. Sidebar: Scale X 0.05, Y 0.25, Z 0.5: a tile 10 cm thick, 50 cm wide, 1 m tall. Location X -4, Z 0.5: standing on the floor.
    2. b
      Physics › Rigid Body: Active, Shape Box, Mass 1, Surface Response › Friction 1.
    3. c
      Material › New › Ivory › Hex F2E8D5. F2: Domino.

    You should now see: one tall thin tile standing at X -4, pale, with an Active Box rigid body.

    Why friction 1 on a domino?

    A falling domino pivots on its bottom edge. With low friction the bottom edge skids backwards as the top goes forward and the tile slides instead of tipping, which breaks the chain. Friction 1 pins the edge so the tile rotates.

  3. Eleven copies

    The viewport.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Domino selected. Shift+D, X, 0.6, Enter: a copy 60 cm along.
    2. b
      Eleven times: twelve dominoes, Domino to Domino.011, from X -4 to X 2.6.

    You should now see: a row of twelve tiles with 50 cm of air between their faces. Checkpoint D below.

    Why 0.6?

    A 1 m tile that tips over reaches 1 m along the floor, so the next face must be closer than that; 0.6 between centres is 0.5 between faces, half the height. Closer is faster but the tiles lean on each other; further is slower and a harder knock; further than 1 m and the chain stops. The widget below lets you try it.

    Domino spacing

    Twelve 1 m tiles. Drag the gap between faces and press Run.

  4. A ramp

    Add › Mesh › Plane, then the N sidebar › Item tab, Properties editor (bottom right) › the blue orbit Physics tab (near the bottom of the tab column) and Properties editor › the red sphere Material tab.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Add › Mesh › Plane. Sidebar: Scale 1.5, 1.5, 1.5 (a 3 m square). Rotation Y 25. Location X -7, Z 0.63.
    2. b
      Physics › Rigid Body: Passive, Shape Mesh.
    3. c
      Material › New › Ramp › Hex 8A9BB0. F2: Ramp.

    You should now see: a tilted square whose low edge touches the floor at X -5.64, just before the first domino, and whose high edge is 1.26 m up.

    Where do 0.63 and -5.64 come from?

    A 3 m square tilted 25° spans 3 × cos 25° = 2.72 m along X and rises 3 × sin 25° = 1.27 m. Centre it at Z 0.63 (half the rise) and the low edge sits on the floor; centre it at X -7 and the low edge lands at -7 + 1.36 = -5.64, 36 cm before the first domino.

  5. A heavy ball

    Add › Mesh › UV Sphere, the Add … panel that opens bottom-left of the viewport (click its title if it is folded), then Properties editor (bottom right) › the blue orbit Physics tab (near the bottom of the tab column) and Properties editor › the red sphere Material tab.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Add › Mesh › UV Sphere. Panel: Radius 0.3, Location X -8.1, Z 1.5. Just above the top of the ramp. Right-click › Shade Smooth.
    2. b
      Physics › Rigid Body: Active, Shape Sphere, Mass 5. Surface Response › Bounciness 0.
    3. c
      Material › New › Blue › Hex 2B6CB0. F2: Ball.

    You should now see: a blue ball hanging above the high end of the ramp.

    Why 5 kg, and why Bounciness 0?

    The ball has to knock over a 1 kg tile from a rolling start, so it is five times the mass. Bounciness 0 means it lands on the ramp and rolls instead of hopping: a hop on a 25° slope can send it off the side. Sphere is the exact shape for a ball, and rolling needs an exact shape.

  6. Play the run

    the Timeline along the bottom of the window and the viewport.

    Predict first: Twelve tiles at about 9 frames each: which frame will the last one fall on, if the first tips at 61?

    Do this:

    1. a
      Timeline: End 192. Shift+←, then Space.
    2. b
      The ball drops onto the ramp and rolls, faster and faster. Frame 48: it reaches the first domino. Frame 61: the first one is past tipping.
    3. c
      A wave runs down the row, about 9 frames a tile. Frame 150: the last one goes. Space to pause, Shift+← to rewind.

    You should now see: twelve dominoes down in order, a ball stopped by the row it started. Not matching? See the chain stops, the ball misses or the tiles slide instead of tipping.

    Why does each one fall?

    A standing tile is balanced on its bottom face. The one before it only has to push its top past the point where its centre is over the edge; after that gravity does the rest, and it arrives at the next tile with speed. That is a chain reaction: a small push, then energy stored in every standing tile, released one at a time.

  7. Bake the run

    Properties editor › the Scene tab.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Scene tab › Rigid Body World › Cache: End 192. Bake.
    2. b
      Delete Bake appears. Scrub to any frame: the run is locked in.

    You should now see: the Cache panel showing Delete Bake.

  8. Light and camera

    The Outliner, the Data tabs, the N sidebar › Item tab and the World tab.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Light: Sun, Strength 3, Rotation 50, 10, -60. World Color Hex B8C6D4. The same recipe as Step 14.
    2. b
      Camera: Location X -3.5, Y -12, Z 4. Rotation X 74, Y 0, Z -5. Focal Length 32.
    3. c
      Numpad 0: the row across the picture, the ramp and the ball at the left.

    You should now see: the camera view with the ramp at the left and all twelve tiles in frame. Checkpoint E below.

  9. A still and the movie

    The Render tab, the Output tab, the Render menu.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Frame box: 100, the wave halfway down the row. Render tab › Cycles, Max Samples 64. F12. Image › Save As › Lab9B_Dominoes_YourName_render.
    2. b
      Render Engine back to EEVEE. Output tab: Resolution 50%, Media Type Video, Container MPEG-4.
    3. c
      Render › Render Animation. 192 frames. Ctrl+S.

    You should now see: a still of the wave and a file called 0001-0192.mp4.

  10. Save and hand in

    The File menu and SEQTA.

    Do this:

    1. a
      Ctrl+S in both files. The title bar loses its asterisk.
    2. b
      Upload to SEQTA — Lab 9: Lab9A_Sweeper_YourName.blend, Lab9B_Dominoes_YourName.blend, and the two renders and two movies that go with them.
    3. c
      Not finished? Upload what you have and say which step you reached.

    You should now see: six files in SEQTA.

End of the lab. Save both files, upload, and then try an extension.

Part 6

Finished early? Pick one

Tools: everything above, used again.

Each one is a small experiment. Change one thing, predict, play, compare. Write the answer in a sentence.

Heavier blocks, lighter blocks

Part A. Select all fifteen blocks (click one, then Select › Select All by Type › Mesh and Ctrl-click the Sweeper and Floor to drop them). Physics tab: Mass 1, then Object › Rigid Body › Copy from Active so all fifteen get it. Delete Bake, play. Lighter blocks bounce off the bar and tumble further; heavier ones (200) just slide. Why does the sweeper not slow down either way? (Step 8’s Why.)

Slippery floor

Part A. Floor and all blocks: Friction 0.1. Delete Bake, play. The pile keeps sliding after frame 130 and some blocks go off the far edge. Use the friction widget under Step 6 to predict how far before you play it.

A bouncy sweep

Part A. All blocks: Surface Response › Bounciness 0.8. Blocks hop over the bar. Now set the sweeper’s Bounciness to 0.8 as well and compare: a collision uses both objects’ numbers.

Turn the corner

Part B. Dominoes 6 to 11: select them and rotate the group R Z 30 around domino 6 (set the pivot: click domino 6, Shift+S › Cursor to Selected, then pivot point › 3D Cursor in the header). Does the wave go round the bend? Real domino runs curve by keeping each face square to the one before.

Faster ball, slower ball

Part B. Ball Z 2.5 and the ramp Rotation Y 40, Location Z 0.96 (half of 3 × sin 40°): a steeper, higher start. Or Ball Mass 0.5: too light to knock the first tile? Delete Bake and play each time. Which matters more for knocking the first tile over: mass or speed?

Bigger gaps

Part B. Select Domino.001 to Domino.011 and move them so the gap between centres is 0.9 m (select all eleven, S X 1.5 with the pivot on Domino: Shift+S › Cursor to Selected on the first tile, pivot › 3D Cursor). Delete Bake, play. Count the frames per tile against the 9 you measured. Then 1.1 m: the chain stops; the widget under Step 20 says why.

Something’s not right

Find the problem that matches yours.

F2 only shows a box for a name; I can’t find Sweeper (or Floor, Block, Domino, Ramp, Ball)

That box is the whole point. F2 is Rename: the box is where you type the object’s new name, then Enter. Sweeper, Floor, Block, Domino, Ramp and Ball are names this lab gives to things you have just made; they are not tools. If a step says “F2: Block”, it means: press F2, type Block, press Enter. (F3 is a different key, Search; close it with Esc if you opened it.)

I typed Scale numbers but it moved, or it grew instead of moving

Wrong row. The sidebar has three groups: Location (metres), Rotation (degrees), Scale (no unit). Ctrl+Z and find the right box.

The block (or the bar) is half under the floor

Location Z must equal Scale Z for a cube: 0.25 for the block, 0.3 for the sweeper, 0.5 for a domino. A block that starts inside the floor is kicked out on frame 1 and the sweep goes wrong.

The blocks fall through the floor

The floor has no Rigid Body, or its Type is Active. Click the Floor: Physics tab must show Rigid Body, Passive, Mesh (Step 7). If the floor is Active it falls too, and you will see it drop away.

The bar passes straight through the blocks

Three checks on the Sweeper (Step 8): it has a Rigid Body; Type Passive; Animated ticked. Without Animated, a Passive body is frozen where it was on frame 1 even though the keyframes move the mesh; the physics never sees it move. Then: play from frame 1 (Shift+Left, Space). Scrubbing does not run the physics.

The blocks fly everywhere, or jitter before the bar arrives

Blocks that start overlapping each other or the floor get pushed apart violently on frame 1. Check the copies: 1.5 m apart in X, 2.5 m in Y (Step 9), Z 0.25. A block inside another block: delete it. Jittering with nothing touching: the collision margin; Scene tab › Rigid Body World › Substeps Per Frame 20 calms it.

Not fifteen blocks

Outliner: Block, Block.001 … Block.014 is fifteen. Too many: a Shift+D with no move leaves a copy on top of the original (Ctrl+Z, or delete the extra). Too few: one Shift+D was skipped; copy the last block again.

The copies have no physics or no colour

You copied before Steps 5 and 6, or made new cubes instead of Shift+D. Click a copy: it must show Rigid Body and the Red material. Quickest fix: delete the copies (keep the one with everything on it) and redo Step 9.

The sidebar boxes are orange

Orange means changed but not keyed. Press I while the mouse is over the viewport. Moving to another frame without pressing I throws the change away.

The sweeper does not move when I scrub or play

It needs two keys: Y -9 on frame 1 and Y 9 on frame 130 (Steps 10 and 11). Click it and count the diamonds in the timeline. If both are on frame 1, you typed 9 before changing the frame: go to 130, type Y 9, press I.

I changed a mass (or a key) and nothing changed

The simulation is baked. Scene tab › Rigid Body World › Cache › Delete Bake, then play from frame 1, then Bake again. A baked simulation is frozen on purpose.

Numpad 0 shows nothing useful

Check the camera’s numbers in the sidebar (Part A: Location -17, -14, 9; Rotation 69, 0, -49; 32 mm. Part B: -3.5, -12, 4; 74, 0, -5; 32 mm). If you typed into the wrong object, click Camera in the Outliner first. No numpad? Click the camera icon in the little column under the gizmo.

The render is almost black, or the far end is dark

The light is still a Point: Data tab › Sun, Strength 3 (Step 14). A point light fades with distance; a sun does not. World Color B8C6D4 for the sky.

Render Animation makes pictures, not a movie

Media Type is still Image. Output tab › Output panel › Media Type › Video, Container MPEG-4, then render again. The movie lands in the folder shown in the output path box.

The ball misses the first domino, or rolls off the ramp

Ball X -8.1, Y 0, Z 1.5 and the ramp at X -7, Y 0, Z 0.63, Rotation Y 25 (Steps 21, 22): the ball must be above the high edge, and both on Y 0 with the dominoes. Bounciness 0 on the ball; a bouncy ball hops sideways. Shape Sphere: a Box-shaped ball does not roll.

The chain stops partway

A gap wider than the tile is tall (1 m), or one tile out of line. Check the X positions: -4, -3.4, -2.8 … 2.6, all at Y 0. If the ball is too slow to tip the first tile, raise it: Ball Z 2.5. If the first falls and the second does not, the second tile may be rotated: Rotation 0, 0, 0 on all of them.

The tiles slide instead of tipping

Friction 1 on the dominoes and the floor (Steps 18, 19). With low friction the bottom edge skids backward instead of pivoting.

I can’t orbit (no middle mouse button)

Drag on the coloured gizmo itself to orbit. Or turn on Edit › Preferences › Input › Emulate 3 Button Mouse, then Alt + left-drag orbits.

I have no number pad (Numpad 0)

Use the camera icon in the column under the gizmo, or View › Cameras › Active Camera. Or turn on Edit › Preferences › Input › Emulate Numpad; then the 1, 2, 3 keys change the view instead of the select mode.

Nine quick questions

Pick an answer to lock it in. You’ll find out straight away whether you’re right.

1The sweeper is Passive with Animated ticked. What happens when it meets twenty kilograms of blocks?

Right. Keyframes win: an Animated body is moved by the animation and the physics only reads where it is.

Not quite. Animated means the keyframes decide where it is every frame; the physics cannot slow it. It pushes everything Active out of its way.

2Which collision shape should a cube-shaped block use?

Right. A box is exactly a box. Mesh is slower and no better for a cube.

Not quite. Box fits a cube exactly and is the fastest shape. Mesh is for shapes with holes, like a cup.

3A plane used as a floor gets Shape Mesh. Why not Box?

Right. The plane itself is the shape.

Not quite. A box needs an inside. A plane has none, so Mesh uses the plane as it is.

4What does Location Z = Scale Z do for a cube?

Right. A cube is centred on its origin, so half its height (Scale Z) lifts the bottom to zero.

Not quite. Scale Z is half the cube’s height, measured from the centre; Location Z of the same number puts the bottom on the floor.

5A sidebar box turns orange after you type a value. What does that mean?

Right. Press I to key it or the change is lost when the frame changes.

Not quite. Orange = changed but not keyed. Yellow = keyed on this frame. Green = animated, no key here.

6The blocks slide on after the sweeper stops at frame 130. The most likely setting to change is…

Right. Friction is grip; at 0.5 a pushed block skates, at 1 it stays.

Not quite. Mass does not change how far a block skids (grip and momentum both scale with it). Friction does.

7Why does a baked simulation ignore a changed mass?

Right. A bake is frozen on purpose so rendering is reliable.

Not quite. Baking stores all the frames. To see a change: Delete Bake, play from frame 1, Bake again.

8Twelve 1 m dominoes with 0.5 m between faces fell at about 9 frames each. Make the gap 1.1 m. What happens?

Right. A 1 m tile reaches 1 m along the floor; it cannot cross a 1.1 m gap.

Not quite. A tile can only reach as far as it is tall. A gap longer than 1 m stops the chain at the first tile.

9Cycles or EEVEE, GPU or CPU: which pair is which?

Right. The Word lab muddled them. Renderer changes the picture; device only changes the speed.

Not quite. Cycles and EEVEE are the two renderers. GPU/CPU is a device choice for Cycles and only changes how fast it runs.

Check yourself

Tick each one you can honestly do now. Anything left unticked is what to ask about next lesson.

Think about it

The sweeper never slows down, however many blocks it pushes. Is that realistic? What would a real bulldozer do, and which rigid body type would you give it to find out? And: in Part B, the ball is five times the mass of a tile. What would happen with a ball of 0.2 kg, and why?

Upload to SEQTA — Lab 9

Upload Lab9A_Sweeper_YourName.blend and Lab9B_Dominoes_YourName.blend, the two Cycles stills (Lab9A_Sweeper_YourName_render.png, Lab9B_Dominoes_YourName_render.png) and the two movies (0001-0160.mp4 and 0001-0192.mp4). Part A should contain a Sweeper (Passive, Animated, Box, two keys), a Floor (Passive, Mesh) and fifteen blocks (Active, Box, 20 kg, friction 1), baked. Part B: twelve dominoes, a ramp, a ball (Active, Sphere, 5 kg), baked.

Due one week from when this lab was handed out.

Teacher notes

Timing

Two lessons. Lesson 1: Parts 1–3 (the sweeper built, given physics, keyed, played, baked). Lesson 2: Part 4 (light, camera, still, movie) and Part B. The 160-frame EEVEE movie at 50%% takes 2–4 minutes on a school machine; the 192-frame one about the same. The Cycles stills at 64 samples take about a minute each.

What this lab is

The Word lab Lab 9A — Gravity and movement rebuilt as Part A, with every “by eye” move replaced by a number, every setting explained, and the two collision-shape mistakes corrected; and a Part B (the domino run) written to replace the Word lab’s Section B, which was only a link to a YouTube video. It is Lab 9 in the HTML series (the Word file called it 9A and 9B; the file names keep A and B).

Audit of the source lab (Lab 9A, Word)

Correctness. “Pane” for Plane. Step 6: Shape Mesh on a small cube, where Box is exact and much faster (Mesh collision on a cube is the single most common cause of slow or jittery rigid-body scenes); step 9 gives the cuboid Mesh as well. Step 7 “increase the friction, damping translation and the rotation” with a screenshot showing 0.314 and 0.608: damping is a brake applied every frame to the block’s own motion, which has nothing to do with friction against the floor and makes the blocks look as if they are moving through syrup; this lab uses friction 1 and leaves damping at its defaults, and the friction widget explains what the number does. Step 16 “If you have a powerful GPU, use GPU, otherwise use EEVE” conflates the renderer (Cycles / EEVEE) with the Cycles device (GPU / CPU). The scene is never baked and the frame range is never set, so the Word lab’s render runs to frame 250 with 120 frames of nothing.

Completeness. No amounts anywhere: “press S then X to scale”, “press s to scale”, “G then Y” and “G then Z” to move with no distance, “add a small cube… press G to position it accordingly”, “move it towards the other end”. Step 15 “press shift+d to duplicate it” once, with no count and no placement. Step 14 “change the material” and step 17 “change the colour and lighting as necessary” are screenshots. No camera step at all; “render your file” does not say still or animation, or where the output goes. Section B is a video link.

Clarity. Step numbers run 1, 2, 3, 3, 4, 5, 6 … Step 4 says “part of the cuboid is below” and step 5 fixes it by “select the plane, press G then Z to grab the cuboid” (two objects in one sentence). Steps 10–13 use “keyframe 130” for frame 130.

Pedagogy and year level. The Word lab never says what Active, Passive or Animated mean, so students cannot predict or debug; the three are the whole point of the lab, and here they get a card, a table, a Why on each step, and a quiz question. The by-eye moves mean no two students’ scenes match and the teacher cannot tell a wrong setting from a different layout. Section B outsources half the lab to a video.

Design decisions

  • Exact numbers everywhere (Scale 5, 0.3, 0.3; Y -9 to 9; a 5 × 3 field 1.5 and 2.5 m apart). The sweep then has a known speed (3.4 m/s), known contact frames (48, 70, 84) and a known end state (all fifteen at the far edge), so the checkpoints are checkable.
  • Box for the blocks and the sweeper, Mesh for the planes, Sphere for the ball, each with a reason on the step and the shapes card.
  • Friction 1, no damping. The friction widget under Step 6 shows the skid distance formula so the number is not magic.
  • Materials before copying (Step 5 before Step 9).
  • Bake before render, and the cache end set, in both parts.
  • Part B uses only tools from Part A plus a Sphere shape, a rotated plane and Bounciness; it adds a chain reaction, which is the physics idea the Word lab’s video was about. The ramp numbers are derived on the step (3 m × cos 25°, 3 m × sin 25°); the domino-spacing widget shows why 0.6 m works and 1.1 m does not.

Tested values

Both parts were built from these steps in Blender 5.2 (bpy) and simulated: Part A, all fifteen blocks are moved by the sweeper, first contact on frame 48, every block between Y 9.5 and 10.8 at frame 160, none off the floor. Part B, the ball reaches the first domino at frame 48, the first tile passes 45° at frame 61 and the twelfth at frame 150, 8–10 frames per tile. The checkpoint pictures, the hero still and the filmstrips were rendered from those files (Cycles, 32 samples). Blender 4.2 or newer: Media Type › Video in Step 17 is the 4.5+ wording (on 4.2 it is File Format › FFmpeg Video). Pressing I over the viewport inserts Location, Rotation and Scale keys at once in 4.1+; on older versions a menu appears and the step says to choose Location. The two finished .blend files are supplied with this lab.

Where students usually get stuck

Dragging the sweeper instead of typing Y 9 (Step 11). Pressing I with the mouse over the sidebar instead of the viewport. Typing Y 9 before changing the frame, so both keys land on frame 1 (the fix the sweeper does not move). Forgetting Animated on the sweeper (Step 8), which gives a bar that scrubs through the blocks. Shift+D without a move, which leaves two blocks on top of each other and an explosion on frame 1. Changing a mass without Delete Bake (Step 13). Leaving Media Type on Image (Step 17). In Part B: the ball at Y 0.5 instead of 0, so it rolls past the row; a domino rotated by a stray R.

Quiz answers

1 Pushes them at its keyframed speed. 2 Box. 3 No thickness. 4 Bottom on the floor. 5 Changed, not keyed. 6 Friction. 7 Delete Bake, play, Bake. 8 Lands flat. 9 Renderers vs device.
